Penny Wigram

Penny Wigram

London

Penny Wigram  

Madness is an integral part of the human condition. We are only just beginning, with the help of modern science and post-psychoanalytic thought to unravel the mysteries of the human mind and its effect on our psychological and physiological well-being. Before psychoanalysis and neuroscience, with all the medical advances now available, madness was the subject of myth, legend and literature, and was feared and reviled as well as romanticized. The stories of so many great artists and writers whose genius has bordered on madness reminds us of the fine line we tread as humans between a managed and fruitful life and one that spins out of control into the darker areas of the mind. Is madness relative? What some people perceive as madness is perceived by others as mystical or creative. Certain rituals and ways of behaving are considered normal in one culture and mad in another. The problem is, who decides?

As therapists we hope to be referred the ‘healthy’ neurotic patients with strong enough ego strength and intellect to benefit from psychodynamic treatment, and who will not invade and disturb our own areas of personal madness. However, this does not always work so neatly, and we need the tools at least to begin to understand, and to be able to flag up those whose symptoms may not benefit from our kind of therapy.

Editorial

Janine Sternberg

Janine Sternberg

[janinesternberg@btinternet.com]

Janine Sternberg  

As regular readers of the BJP are aware, Rachel Winter resigned as Editor of the BJP with the production of BJP 23.2 and this edition marks the beginning of the ‘new order’ that she referred to in her last editorial. Yet, because of the ‘time warp effect’ she wrote of, many of the very interesting articles that appear in this issue were in fact accepted and worked on during her time as editor. Indeed it is fitting that the influence of the previous editor lingers on some time after the end of their actual tenure, influencing the continuing life of the Journal in all sorts of ways. Readers of the BJP have much to be grateful for from Rachel Winter's committed stewardship. She displayed a dedication to the Journal and all that it stands for, and worked hard to ensure the best possible copy for each edition produced under her editorship. In this she was aided by an active Editorial Board and I am delighted that all members of that Board have continued to be involved in the ongoing life of the BJP and they have been joined by some members of the BAP Journal Editorial Board. It is that combined group, steered by me in the role of Editorial Board Coordinator, who have been responsible for all the hard work that has been involved in producing this issue, showing, I think, how much can be achieved by collective effort when those involved are concentrating on the task rather than on perpetuating traditional lines of demarcation. The comments on the papers below are the work of individual Editorial Board members.

This edition displays the breadth of topics that has always characterized the BJP. Ideas about perversion are addressed in multiple ways: in Cheese's thought-provoking clinical paper, in Valentine's arresting exploration of a film that introduces the viewer to sadomasochism and perverse states of mind, and also in Mendoza's careful delineation of perversity from diversity. By way of contrast we have Williams's compelling exploration of creativity, Reeves's scholarly exploration of a Winnicott paper and Sacks's fascinating account of the connections between CBT and Bi-logic (both possibly rather unfamiliar areas for BJP readers)

Jack Nathan  

Personality disorders are an ill-defined group of psychopathological conditions that are increasingly seen as one of the main domains of NHS dynamic psychotherapy. The authors discuss some of the concepts that underlie the diagnosis though it can most easily be understood as severe non-psychotic pathology. Psychoanalytic theory has suggested several paradigms to understand and treat such conditions, and most of these rely on interpretation as the central therapeutic agent. The authors argue in this paper that therapists may need to consider the use of limit setting with patients with personality disorder where dangerous acting out may occur. This runs counter to the principles of therapeutic neutrality, and yet the limit setting may be a prerequisite to an effective therapeutic encounter.

The BJP: More than Just A Journal

Carola Thorpe

Carola Thorpe

Flat 10, Old Court House, 24 Old Court Place, London W8 4PD

Carola Thorpe  

Dear Editor

The purchase of the BJP secures a valuable asset for the BAP and Black-well Publishing (the latter now taken over by John Wiley & Sons). I would like to consider what it is that has actually been acquired and how it should be treated.

Whilst legally and financially the BAP is now a co-owner with the publishing company, I believe the BAP, in particular, has also inherited something very precious, which is the symbolic ownership of the Journal by a self-selected group of organisations representing our profession.

It was Bob Hinshelwood's innovative, creative, courageous commitment that gave British psychoanalytic psychotherapy a journal that was open to papers from anyone working within the psychoanalytic tradition, so long as they met editorial standards. The Journal survived the UKCP/BCP split, maintaining its editorial policy, and for 22 years it has acted as both a bridge and a container for our differences and divides.

Behind this achievement lay an interesting organisational structure. At its inception Bob Hinshelwood invited the relevant associations to be Sponsoring Organisations. Those that decided to join the venture entered into an unwritten contract between themselves and the Journal: in exchange for the support of a block subscription for the entire membership of each organisation, an editorial seat was secured. This ensured that any organisation that wanted to be involved had a voice and was linked directly into the creative endeavour. I think this structure gave the six organisations a sense of ownership and responsibility towards this unique over-arching professional container.

How will that legacy be treated? The Sponsoring Organisations are now to be called Founding Organisations reflecting the change in their relationship to the Journal as they are released from the requirement to have a block subscription. With the dissolution of this arrangement, the unwritten contract that has been effective for the past 22 years ceases. Whilst the FOs are to retain their places on the Editorial Board and others may be invited to join, these appear now to be entirely in the ‘gift’ of the owners. Whilst the arrangement may look much the same, there will have been a subtle but significant change in the structure with this shift of power to the owners. What I am saying and believe is that the original structure allowed for the differences in our professional world to be aired and worked through without breaking the container.

Clinical Material: Two Extracts from George Eliot's Middlemarch

Extract One

For to Dorothea, after that toy-box history of the world adapted to young ladies which had made the chief part of her education, Mr Casaubon's talk about his great book was full of new vistas; and this sense of revelation, this surprise of a nearer introduction to Stoics and Alexandrians, as people who had ideas not totally unlike her own, kept in abeyance for the time her usual eagerness for a binding theory which could bring her own life and doctrine into strict connection with that amazing past, and give the remotest sources of knowledge some bearing on her actions. That more complete teaching would come - Mr Casaubon would tell her all that: she was looking forward to higher initiation in ideas, as she was looking forward to marriage, and blending her dim conceptions of both. It would be a great mistake to suppose that Dorothea would have cared about any share in Mr Casaubon's learning as mere accomplishment; for though opinion in the neighbourhood of Freshitt and Tipton had pronounced her clever, that epithet would not have described her to circles in whose more precise vocabulary cleverness implies mere aptitude for knowing and doing, apart from character. All her eagerness for acquirement lay within that full current of sympathetic motive in which her ideas and impulses were habitually swept along.

Susan Budd

Susan Budd

The Provost's Lodgings, Queen's Lane, Oxford OX1 4AW [susanbudd@mail.com]

Susan Budd  

I last read Middlemarch as a set text at school, and was pleased to be given an incentive by the BJP to re-read it. It turned out to be much, much funnier, and more psychologically and morally even-handed, than I had remembered. I can see why Freud liked to read George Eliot; she is an anatomist of the divided self, the inner conflict between how we wish we were and how we find ourselves behaving.

However, the two passages which we are to consider deal with Dorothea Brooke, the person in the book who seems to me to be the least psychologically credible, and about whom the authorial voice is most ambiguous. I remember a conversation with a girl in the English set in the year above me at school, warning me about the book. ‘It's absolutely preposterous,’ she said. ‘It starts off with two sisters dividing their mother's jewels between them. Celia wants them; Dorothea rejects them because she thinks that she shouldn't want them, but makes her younger sister feel greedy, and then feels guilty about it.’ She found Dorothea unconvincing and unendearing. Henry James, who was critical of some aspects of Middlemarch when he reviewed it in 1873, thought Dorothea ‘the great achievement of the book’, ‘that perfect flower of conception … an indefinably moral elevation’. Doubtless then we were callow adolescents, but to me, even now, Dorothea seems both less believable and less admirable than the author would seem to think.

Clinical Commentary XXXV

Emma Letley

Emma Letley

[emma@letley24.freeserve.co.uk]

Emma Letley  

This section departs from the more usual BJP format in taking for consideration not clinical material but extracts from a Victorian novel - George Eliot's Middlemarch (1871-2). As is the case with many novels, and especially with Eliot's last two great books, Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda, the text is peopled with personalities whose characters, experience of the world and self-experience may with validity be viewed thorough a psychoanalytic lens. Freud much admired Eliot's novels drawing on Adam Bede in The Interpretation of Dreams (Freud 1900) and, remarking of Middlemarch, that, in Ernest Jones's words, ‘It greatly illuminated important aspects of his relations with Martha’ (Jones 1953-57). It would be fascinating to know what these aspects of his marital situation might be. It is also known that Freud gave Eliot's novels as gifts to his friends (Ingram l988; Rotenberg l999).

At a time when the need for strict confidentiality makes it difficult to publish clinical material in the conventional form, perhaps clinician-writers in the field may feel encouraged by this BJP initiative to turn to literature to explore, illuminate or exemplify analytic work for purposes of publication.

Commentators were asked to consider the two extracts below from the novel. After a rapid decline in popularity following the author's death, Middlemarch, often seen as the first truly psychological novel, has retrieved its reputation as a masterpiece and as a great exposition of the anatomy of marriage.

The first extract concerns the attitude of the heroine, Dorothea Brooke, to the academic interests of the elderly cleric, Edward Casaubon. The second piece, after her marriage to Casaubon and during her disastrous honeymoon in Rome, focuses on Dorothea's early interactions with Mr Casaubon's young cousin, Will Ladislaw, a Shelleyan or Romantic figure.

The two vignettes thus offer views before and after marriage, with the second piece foreshadowing the possibility of the heroine's second marriage to Will Ladislaw; this takes place after Casaubon's death despite his attempt to prevent it by adding a codicil to his will depriving Dorothea of her fortune in the event of her marrying Will.

Jan Lee: A Tribute

Laurence Roberts

Laurence Roberts

[email: laurence.roberts@virgin.net]

Laurence Roberts  

Jan Lee, psychoanalytic psychotherapist and Jungian analyst, has died from metastatic breast cancer. She had worked for the last 25 years as a therapist in a variety of settings, within charitable organizations and with patients who do not usually access private therapy, including bereavement work, youth counselling, student counselling and running a community-based counselling service. For 11 years she was a senior NHS psychotherapist in primary care in Ealing, West London.

Jan was an Exhibitioner in Modern Languages at Newnham College, Cambridge. She later trained as a counsellor at South West London Polytechnic, and then completed analytic trainings at The Guild of Psychotherapists and the Society for Analytical Psychology. She greatly valued her connections with both Guild and SAP, ‘like having two homes, different in character and ambience and situated in different localities’. She contributed to the SAP's Public Programme Committee, represented the Society on the BPC Council, and was recently co-opted onto the Council of the SAP. At The Guild she was Chair successively of the External Affairs Committee and the Low Fee Clinic. The latter was particularly close to her heart, in bringing psychotherapy to a disadvantaged South London borough. She played an important role in improvements to make the Clinic more accessible to those with disabilities.

She was in private practice in Chiswick, working variously from Brief Focal Psychotherapy to long-term four-times-weekly analysis. In her teaching work she drew on passions for world mythology, Sufism, Shamanism, the I Ching, astronomy, astrological symbolism, film and music. She was a wife, a mother, a grandmother, a colleague and a good friend to many.

Such a list - an incomplete one - perhaps gives an indication of the gusto with which Jan committed herself. Having survived polio as a child, she believed in life and in the beauty of life. She was a perfectionist with a desire to get things right. Once committed, she followed through totally. Her energy impacted on so many people she encountered, yet this energy, far from exhausting, was an inspiration, as was her kindness, her warmth, her ‘way with an anxious soul’. At her Celebration a friend described her as being like a candle which burns perfectly, maintaining its shape, until finally it burns itself out.

Diversity and Perversity

Steven Mendoza

Steven Mendoza

19 Saville Road, Twickenham TW1 4BQ. [email: steven@thornfield.vispa.com]

Steven Mendoza  

Biological diversity is presented as a model of psychic diversity. Perversity, the general form of perversion which pervades, to some extent, the psyches of us all, is not presented as a diversity of lifestyle, as political correct-ness might have it. It is presented as a psychopathology causing suffering and needing help. The reprehension of perversity is suggested, through the work of Bion, as itself an aspect of perversity. The difficulties of analysing perversity through the general condition of narcissism is addressed emotionally through the universality of some measure of narcissism and theoretically through the work of Bion on ‘without-ness’, frustration and the disappointment of constant conjunction, and through Meltzer's distinction between polymorphous and perverse and through his concept of aesthetic conflict.

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

Writing the editorial creates a sort of time warp effect, because the 6-month lead time of the Journal means that what I am writing now, you will be reading some 3-4 months later. When I was writing the editorial for 23(1), for example, the Journal was about to be sold but it was not yet certain which of the offers then ‘on the table’ would be accepted. By the time you came to read it, the sale was complete and the whole situation had changed; new owners, new publishers, new production team and so on. Similarly, by the time you read this editorial, a new Editor will be in post. I am extremely sad to be leaving the Journal but it is appropriate that a new order should start with a new Editor.

As you read this, the farewell party for Artesian Books will also have taken place and I hope to have joined with many of our loyal authors, editorial advisors and other ‘friends of the BJP’, together with those of our erstwhile sister journal ‘Psychoanalysis and History’, to celebrate a remarkable achievement. I have several times referred in the pages of this journal to the creative vision of Bob Hinshelwood, when he brought together all those organisations who were willing, to set up the co-operative venture that was the BJP. Over 22 years the BJP has grown and flourished to become the most successful and widely read British journal in its field and I have no doubt it will continue to develop and improve under its new owners.

Professor R D Hinshelwood, the founder and ‘onlie begetter’ of these journals, is an eminent Kleinian analyst, scholar, writer and teacher whose career is well documented. As owner of the BJP he has always had a very light touch as he strongly believes in a healthy tolerance of disparate views and is not someone who wishes to assert the hegemony of his particular school of thought. He is well known for his generous encouragement of authors and I may add, editors too. (‘The Flower’, Herbert 1663)

Over autumn 2005 and spring 2006 the Maya Centre put on a series of eight lectures on the subject of resilience. We were invited to publish a selection from this series in the BJP.

The Maya Centre, founded in 1984 in Islington, North London, provides free psychodynamic counselling for women who are on poverty-level incomes (below £8000 for those with no dependants, £11000 with dependants), who have not completed higher education, and who have received no previous long-term psychotherapy or counselling. The current work of the Centre focuses on the mothers of young children and teenagers, older women, women in situations of violence, Black, Irish, Turkish and Somali women. For the last two, counselling is given in their mother tongue. The Centre employs seven part-time counsellors and psychotherapists and is a charity entirely dependent on the public and private funding it is able to raise.

The clients seen at the Maya Centre find themselves, with few exceptions, in situations of multiple hardship. These stem both from severe stresses in early life, and from additional social disadvantage over time and in the present. Their inner strength, their resilience, has been strongly tested. The ability to survive and prosper is a mysterious and multifaceted issue. It was from a wish to look at these mysteries with a psychoanalytic eye that these lectures grew, bearing in mind that many other discourses can be brought to bear on the subject - social, economic, biological.

This series was put together by Maggie Murray and myself, both Clinical Trustees at the Centre. We were greatly helped by a group of former and current trustees and ‘friends’ of the Maya Centre, Catherine Crowther, Roszika Parker, Margot Waddell and Jean White, and we are very grateful for their contributions.

Pamela Griffiths

Pamela Griffiths  

The final reflective comments of a doctorate student at the end of this book, following completion of her research project, are both a warning and an inspiration to all of us who work in this field. As a ‘well-qualified and experienced clinician’ Philippa found that she was ‘so ignorant of the evidence-based body of knowledge about the psychotherapy process’ (p. 226). Following her research experience she found that her communication with practitioners of different theoretical orientations was enhanced and, of course, there was a ‘refreshing and developmental effect’ on her practice (p. 227). These comments demonstrate the need for this book - a need which has been increasingly recognized over the last decade. Barker, Pistrang and Elliott advocated the importance of the scientist-practitioner model in 1995 noting with enthusiasm the wider range of research methods becoming available to therapists. More recently Loewenthal and Winter (2006) find that in the UK, relative to psychotherapy, it is counselling ‘that has taken a lead in developing practitioner research’ (p. xvii). They note an ambivalence within the psychotherapy discipline to doing research which has led to ‘a lack of relative knowledge of research in psychotherapy’ as well as ‘a history of apparent defensiveness in being evaluated, and a reluctance to work with universities’ (p. xviii). Others, such as Mahrer (2004), are also raising the issue of the need for psychotherapy research.

Thus the book is timely and Lepper and Riding set out very carefully the parameters of the content as well as ways to use the book. It ‘is intended primarily as a teaching and learning resource for both practising and student clinicians’ who wish to carry out ‘clinically relevant research on transcripts of his or her own psychotherapy or counselling sessions’ (p. xiii). They suggest that it is for both the novice and those already engaged in research. Philosophy is rather briefly introduced in the book, which may limit a novice researcher's ability to locate the models within a clear epistemology. The emphasis is rather in setting out the practical details of the method. The four sections (Background to the Field of Psychotherapy Research, The Coding Approaches, The Discourse Approaches and Data Analysis and Documentation) have useful introductions. Examples of practitioner projects and exercises are particularly helpful in understanding the application of the research models. Suggestions for further reading at the end of each chapter enable the reader to pursue further investigations of a particular method.

Richard Duggins  

Models of Madness is the first book in the International Society for the Psychological Treatments of the Schizophrenias and Other Psychoses (ISPS) series. The book's editors, John Read, Loren Mosher and Richard Bentall, alongside contributors from six countries and a variety of backgrounds (including a user of services), have a clear purpose in mind - to end what they describe as the ‘madness’ of biological psychiatry.

The book is structured into three parts. The first part critiques the illness model of ‘schizophrenia’, and passionately challenges the perceived stranglehold that simplistic biological ideology has over mental health services. Read contributes to eight of the 10 chapters in this first part, and his presence guides the reader into a coherent and powerful analysis of the dominant belief that psychotic illness is a biological illness like any other. History, politics and economics are shown to have had much more influence on the development of the concept of schizophrenia than objective evidence. The doctrine that schizophrenia is a chronic, severe and disabling brain disease is shown to possess neither validity nor reliability. Chapters re-examine the research evidence for the aetiology of psychosis, and dispute the key importance of constitutional factors, such as genetics.

The editors contend that the acceptance of a simplistic biogenetic ideology is directly responsible for the unwarranted and destructive pessimism in the treatment of people with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. An important link is made between this biological pessimism and the modern-day enthusiasm and readiness to use routinely treatments such as antipsychotic medications, despite their extensive side-effects. However, in what I consider to be a step too far, Read and Jeffrey Masson present a chapter that suggests this therapeutic nihilism within psychiatry provided fertile ground for eugenics in many countries, and mass murder in Nazi Germany.

The final contribution to this part is by Mosher, Richard Gosden and Sharon Beder, who skilfully expose the increasingly powerful influence drug companies have in promoting a biological view of schizophrenia. The ruthless and pervasive tactics of the drug companies are made clear through the illustration of the recent marketing of atypical anti-psychotics.

Recent years have seen a steadily increasing flow of books and papers re-examining the relationships and conflicts between spirituality, religion and psychoanalysis. Psychoanalysis and Religion in the 21st Century: Competitors or Collaborators? represents a fresh landmark in this process, not least because it is published under the auspices of the Institute of Psychoanalysis. International Journal of Psychoanalysis86, 1611-1626, 2005

The Analyst: His Professional Novel

Laura Ambrosiano

The psychoanalyst needs to be in touch with a community of colleagues; he needs to feel part of a group with which he can share cognitive tension and therapeutic knowledge. Yet group ties are an aspect we analysts seldom discuss. The author defines the analyst's ‘professional novel’ as the emotional vicissitudes with the group that have marked the professional itinerary of every analyst; his relationship with institutions and with theories, and the emotional nuance of these relationships. The analyst's professional novel is the narrative elaboration of his professional autobiography. It is capable of transforming the individual's need to belong and the paths of identification and deidentification. Experience of the oedipal configuration allows the analyst to begin psychic work aimed at gaining spaces of separateness in his relationship with the group. This passage is marked by the work on mourning that separation involves, but also of mourning implicit in the awareness of the representative limits of our theories. Right from the start of analysis, the patient observes the emotional nuance of the analyst's connection to his group and theories; the patient notices how much this connection is governed by rigid needs to belong, and how much freedom of thought and exploration it allows the analyst. The author uses clinical examples to illustrate these hypotheses.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis87, 939-951, 2006

Seeing and being Seen: Narcissistic Pride and Narcissistic Humiliation

John Steiner

Seeing and being seen are important aspects of narcissism, where self-consciousness is always a feature, and one which becomes acute when a patient loses the protection of a narcissistic relationship and is obliged to tolerate a degree of separateness. Having felt hidden and protected, he now feels conspicuous and exposed to a gaze which makes him vulnerable to humiliation. This often has a devastating and unbearable quality to it, particularly when it is felt to arise in retaliation to the patient's own use of gaze to establish a superiority which allowed the patient to look down on others. The need to avoid or cut short such humiliation may be so acute that the patient cannot deal with guilt and other emotions connected with loss which might otherwise be bearable. The author argues that development is impeded unless the patient is able to gain support to make the humiliation better understood and hence better tolerated. He describes some sessions from an analysis to illustrate how, in some analytic situations, much of the patient's concern and many of his defensive maneuvers aim to reduce or to reverse experiences of humiliation. An understanding of the mechanisms involved seemed to enable some development to proceed.

Editorial

Jane Cheshire and Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine

[jane.cheshire@btconnect.com]

[marguerite@f2s.com]

Marguerite Valentine  

This Special Issue on Femininity was conceived following the publication of an edition on Masculinity in BJP 22.1. As guest editors we were intrigued with how ‘femininity’ might be understood, and reading through the papers we were struck by a consistent theme: femininity is no longer seen to originate in, and to be defined by the relationship with man and ‘lack’. It is now understood as also derived from women's relationship with each other, whether as sisters, mothers, lovers or friends. Classical notions of gender based on a binary and symmetrical conceptualization seem no longer theoretically adequate. Thus these writers all adopt a critical perspective in their understanding of how femininity is constructed and how therefore it may be understood.

The questions of binary terms, male/female, masculinity/femininity and active/passive are the same ones that Freud asked us to distinguish between, and he observed that the constructs of masculinity/femininity are the most saturated with the value judgements of each society and period. His theory of sexual identity, which he maintained throughout his life was rooted in the bedrock of psychic bi-sexuality, was both biological and psychological. Throughout his work it moves back and forth between these two dimensions. Since then theorists seem to have come down more firmly on one side or the other of this distinction. For example, Klein thought that intimations of the (sexed) body were innate, informing the nature of earliest phantasy life. And whilst Freud (1937) stated in ‘Analysis Terminable and Interminable’ that for women the desire for a penis is never really given up, Klein mapped the envy that might be felt towards the female/maternal body and its capacities, both physical and psychical. Diametrically opposite to this, Lacan held that the biological body has nothing at all to do with sexuation and the structuring of sexual difference; it is achieved through the setting of limits, the ‘nom du père’, installed through language.

Female Friendship, Fairy Tales, Cinderella Theme, Iconic Significance of Weddings, Oedipal, Pre-Oedipal Analytic Theories, Fantasies, Film Analysis

This paper analyses Muriel's Wedding, a film based on and inspired by the story of ‘Cinderella’. Beginning with a discussion of fairy tales, it argues that interpretations of them are theoretically and culturally specific. Bearing this point in mind, Bettelheim's oedipal analysis of ‘Cinderella’ is compared with an alternative view developed in Muriel's Wedding. Hogan, the film's author and director, posits a different perspective; one where female friendship becomes integral to the psychological development of Muriel. The iconic significance of weddings is also discussed in relation to this. The paper draws on the pre-oedipal theories of Winnicott, and the more recent contributions of analytic feminist and relational theorists. Implicit in this is the contribution that can be made to clinical practice, and the notion there is a dialectical relationship between the fantasies of the inner world and the lived experience of the cultural world.

Christopher Perry  

Jan first encountered Jung when she was 17. She found two volumes in German of his Collected Works at home. She had no idea of how they came to be in the family home. But she read them with her usual single-minded determination. She returned to Jung many years later after journeying through Buddhism and Sufism and trying to grapple with Mysterium Coniunctionis - Jung's last book - an exploration into the processes of differentiating, combining and transcending opposites and differences. For Jan there was no gap between analytical psychology and life. The former offered her a way of life and a way of trying to understand herself and others. Passionate about mining the seam of psyche, Jan was committed to the intense struggle needed to combine the riches of the pluralistic training which she had received at The Guild with the more singular focus on the work of Jung which, to some extent, she found at the Society of Analytical Psychology. But, wishing to unearth ever deeper levels, she embarked on a Clinical Doctorate at the University of Essex. After qualifying in 2001 at the SAP, she soon joined the staff of the Foundation Course, and conducted seminars in the Adult Training on countertransference.

In her daily work, Jan created a containment that combined the strength and flexibility of the bamboo and that enabled her to engage with people in desperate distress with all its attendant psychic pain and internal violence. She worked from a wellspring of compassion, infused by a keen intellect, her feeling-toned thoughts sometimes leavened with a delightful sense of humour - sometimes hidden but always present. Whilst listening intently, Jan relied almost entirely in her work on the inner film running in her mind. She dwelt in the imaginal world. It was from a single image or series of images that she offered her patients and supervisees a thought that might nudge into life a moment of understanding, an awareness of choice, the possibility of life-enhancing change - not always comfortable for the other or herself, because she believed in and knew from experience the mutually transformative effects of deep encounters with the other. Essentially, she supported all those with whom she worked in various capacities through the adventure of finding and being themselves, leading from behind with her own spirit of adventure, and witnessing their journeys.

Jenny Pearson  

The lectures were given in 2002 at the London Centre for Psychotherapy, in an exceptionally popular series devised by the book's editor, Nathan Field. In his Introduction Field describes the enthusiasm that greeted the series:

Within a few weeks of their announcement nearly every seat was sold out for the whole year. No doubt the audience were attracted by the reputation of the speakers on the programme; but even more interesting was the degree of interest that the linking of psychotherapy and spirituality aroused in the counselling and psychotherapy community.

For the practising psychotherapist, the challenge of the area loosely indicated by the word ‘spirituality’ is never far from the daily experience of the consulting room. It makes its presence felt, obliquely but inevitably, in many aspects of the encounter, though historically the traditions of psychoanalytic thinking have offered little acknowledgement of this aspect of human experience. Reasons for such avoidance are not hard to find: at one extreme, we encounter the ‘born again’ patient for whom God is a deeply entrenched superego, reinforcing resistance and anti-libidinal paranoia; at the other, we find the nun practising as therapist who feels unable to wear about her person any object that could be interpreted as a symbol of her religious commitment. The consulting room is kept clear of obvious symbols, allowing for any experience that could be defined as ‘spiritual’ to emerge uncontaminated within the encounter itself. But then, if authentic experience of this order does arise, how and in what language can it be addressed? A safe reference point, if one is needed, is to stay with the mother and baby dyad, but there are times when a ‘holding’ interpretation of this order does not reflect the authentic feel of the session. On the other hand, if we look for a way into such experiences that is not reductive, we soon find ourselves in a place of no words or reference points from which to speak, even among ourselves.

Marco Chiesa  

In this paper the author describes the features and clinical manifestations of specific states of mind, which functioned as psychic retreats in a male homosexual patient. Two main types of retreats emerged in the course of the analysis. The first took the shape of an inanimate object (a spaceship), within which little human contact was allowed to exist. In the second retreat some degree of relating was present, but that mental space was populated with threatening homosexual figures which kept a strong hold on the patient's ego and attacked any meaningful contact established between patient and analyst. The presence of these structures enabled the patient to evade awareness of the injured, paralysed and damaged state in which his internal objects were kept, and to bypass depressive anxieties connected to painful early oedipal conflicts, which included a terrifying maternal introject. The attempt to recruit the analysis into the patient's psychic retreat constituted a central transference manifestation.

Gertrud Mander  

This book is a rich and well-crafted manual for therapists who are working with refugees and want to learn how to engage with the experiences of

304

persecution, violence and exile which are often faced by refugees. It is the outcome of its author's wide experience of working for the Medical Foundation for the Care of Victims of Torture as a psychotherapist and supervisor, and it offers a flexible methodology that was specifically developed to deal with the particular circumstances that characterize the contexts in which different cultural and political backgrounds are usually encountered. In its didactic purpose the book differs deliberately from other books on the refugee experience and therapeutic approaches to helping refugees, such as Therapeutic Care for Refugees by Renos Papadopoulos (2002), who is an expert on the subject.

Blackwell recommends a modification of the psychodynamic approach in regard to frequency, use of the transference, and regression, and he deals consistently with four different levels of experience - the political, the cultural, the interpersonal and the intrapsychic, systematically setting out the multiple issues arising in the course of this kind of work - be that curbing unrealistic expectations, facing one's own ignorance, resolving conflicts with colleagues, working with interpreters, being involved in protection, advocacy and welfare rights, or the need for understanding government policy and legislation with regard to ‘asylum’. Thoughtfully recommending further reading, he also adds pragmatic tips on resources, including the addresses of relevant organizations which may help both the counsellor and the client.

In the section about the therapist's experience Blackwell analyses carefully the client's possible impact and the inevitable feelings of identification, dis-identification, intimidation, discomfort and guilt, which will lead to necessary defences or unconscious acting out. He warns the therapist to guard against unconscious prejudices, to be prepared for the unexpected emotional depth of their encounter with people from similar backgrounds and equally for their totally different experiences of reality - often unmanageable and uncontainable, and hence needing caution, patience and imaginative processing to allow their intensity to become bearable. He describes the difficulties of working with interpreters where split transferences, authority and leadership problems, projections and needs for support will inevitably come to the fore and will require careful handling. Then there are the cultural differences and the various levels of traumatization which need to be faced, while often the outcome is a greater awareness and understanding of how difficult the task of understanding another, and indeed of oneself can be (p. 70).

International Journal of Psychoanalysis87, 329-347, 2006

Being a Psychoanalyst: An Everyday Audacity

Danielle Quinodoz, Candy Aubry, Olivier Bonard, Geneviève Déjussel and Bernard Reith

This paper is the work of five psychoanalysts who came together as a group in order to reflect on their work as analysts. How are we analysts to identify the unconscious resistances that may sometimes hold us back from offering psychoanalysis to some patients? Do these resistances sometimes hamper the inner freedom that we require in order to maintain a psychoanalytic focus once that process is under way? How do we manage from time to time to overcome these resistances or, better, make use of them in order to develop our understanding of the unconscious dynamics that create the link between analyst and patient? The authors discuss these issues with particular reference to clinical situations taken from classic psychoanalytic treatment cases during which the analyst had to find within him- or herself the audacity to be a psychoanalyst. Each clinical situation is different: preliminary interviews, the course of the actual treatment, issues that emerge in the training of candidates. One of the significant features of this group lies in the fact that the participants are at different stages in their development as psychoanalysts (student, associate member, full member, training analyst). This means that their experiences complement one another and encourage a discussion of issues such as how psychoanalysis can be passed on, and the relationship between supervisor and supervisee.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis87, 519-536, 2006

Constructing the Truth: From ‘Confusion of Tongues’ to ‘Constructions in Analysis’

Jacques Press

The author hypothesizes that the papers Freud wrote in the period 1934-9 constitute a final turning point in his work resulting from an attempt to work through, by means of self-analysis, early traumatic elements reactivated by the conditions of his life in the 1930s. The author emphasizes that the ups and downs of Freud's relationship with Sándor Ferenczi and the mourning which followed his death in 1933 played an important role in this traumatic situation. He suggests that, through these last works, Freud pursued a posthumous dialogue with Ferenczi. This working through led Freud, in Moses and Monotheism, to an ultimate revision of his theory of trauma, a revision which the author examines in full, in the light of the works of the Egyptologist, Jan Assmann. A new analytical paradigm emerges: that of constructions in analysis developed in the article of the same name. The activity of construction appears as an alternative to the mutual analysis proposed by Ferenczi and is closely bound up with the notion of historical truth. In psychoanalysis, it would mean constructing a historical truth whose anchoring in the material truth of the past is essential, though it should not be confused with it.

As a Jungian analyst, I understand Dorothea's process both in developmental terms and in terms of the growth of the Self. Dorothea is said to aspire to the acquisition of knowledge and the possession of a life goal, ‘as Saint Theresa did, under the command of an authority that constrained her conscience’. One way of understanding this ‘authority’ is in terms of the Self, a psychosomatic entity which encompasses and propels the various stages of development involved in psychological growth. Martin Schmidt (2005) refers to the relationship of the Self to the ego as ‘a parallel process of both phase and field phenomena’, both being aspects of development involved in psychological growth.

The two vignettes have a dynamic quality. There is a significant passage of time between them and something evolves. Through them, it is possible to capture the effect and influence of one character upon another, either explicitly or by implication.

Astrid Gessert

Astrid Gessert

London

Astrid Gessert  

When, in Eyes Wide Shut, Dr Harford lectures his wife that sexuality does not enter his medical consulting room, and that neither he nor his women patients become distracted by sexual thoughts, she advises him that ‘men don't know what women think’ and proves it by revealing her own erotic reveries about another man.

The enigma of ‘woman’ has never ceased to puzzle both men and women. Freud encountered it in the shape of one of his early patients, Ida Bauer, known as Dora. Treating her for hysterical symptoms Freud mistook her quest for the essence of femininity for a repressed wish to find fulfilment through a man, a misunderstanding that she commented on by abruptly leaving the treatment. Freud's subsequent inquiries into the question of femininity were firmly based on the understanding that it is not anatomy that defines men and women; but what positively marks the difference between the sexes is more difficult to specify. For Freud sexual difference evolved around the question of ‘having’ and ‘not-having’. Man ‘has it’ (the penis), but is threatened by castration. Woman ‘has not got it’, but wants it (in the form of a man or a child). However, Freud came to acknowledge that this logic does not fully account for sexual difference and its manifestations in the clinic. As a legacy of his inquiry he left a question: what does the woman want?

The fact that no conclusive and lasting answer has been found to this question points to some fundamental difficulties with definitions of femininity. In the field of psychoanalysis Jacques Lacan's structural theory leads towards a closer understanding of the nature of these difficulties. Lacan developed and refined his views on the problem of femininity throughout his works and his teaching without, however, presenting them anywhere in the form of a unified and comprehensive theory. Colette Soler has brought together his thoughts on the subject of ‘woman’, paying special attention to his most important texts on this theme: Encore (Lacan 1998) and L'étourdit (Lacan 1973). Through precise and sophisticated analyses she extracts from these and other texts the fundamental parameters that are relevant for developing an understanding of the essence of femininity.

Joanna Rosenthall

Joanna Rosenthall

64 Sotheby Road, London N5 2UT. [email: Jorosenthall@aol.com]

Joanna Rosenthall  

In this paper the writer explores the work with a couple whom she came to think of psychically like Siamese twins, stuck together in order to survive and lacking separate psychic entities with intact coverings. Such a covering is something that we take for granted and which implies that each of us is a separate individual. However, this paper draws attention to the way that some individuals, who have not developed a robust enough sense of identity, might seek a desperate solution, by partnering with someone who shares their dilemma. Being ‘stuck’ together can help stave off intolerable anxieties but tends to raise claustrophobic anxieties. The paper investigates how the underlying anxieties are primitive and serious, and the terrors which are being defended against are often in the area of suicide or breakdown so that, although couple therapy can help to loosen this deadly structure, a more containing intensive individual treatment is likely to be necessary to support the process of individuation.

The Dream of Perfection

Christopher MacKenna

Christopher MacKenna

17 Marylebone Road, London NW1 5LT. [email: cmackenna@stmarylebone.org]

Christopher MacKenna  

Psychoanalytic thinking is suspicious of the notion of perfection, whereas Christian (and other religious) thinking allows an important place to it. Is psychoanalytic hostility justified, or is it part of the depressive mind-set which even some insiders have attributed to the analytic perspective? With help from George Bernard Shaw and Robert Browning, this paper explores the reasons for therapeutic suspicion, but also considers Jesus' teaching about perfection. Following leads offered by Matte Blanco, Jung and others, it argues for the spiritual and therapeutic value of making space for a dream of perfection - but it also highlights the murderous consequences of allowing the dream to become concretized.

Femininity and its Unconscious ‘Shadows’: Gender and Generative Identity in the Age of Biotechnology

Joan Raphael-Leff PHD

Joan Raphael-Leff

[raphael@leff.co.uk]

Joan Raphael-Leff  

Femininity, generative identity, creative agency, biotechnology, fertility treatments, procreation, sexed embodiment, gender representations, erotic desire

This paper locates contemporary conceptualizations of ‘femininity’ in the context of current sociocultural changes. It is argued that today's biotechnological opportunities have immense significance for both psychic interiority and the lived experience of gender, in that they invalidate ‘eternal’ limitations of sex, procreation and embodiment. An explanatory concept, generative identity, is postulated, to account psychologically for the increasing diversity of reproductive patterns. This concept is proposed as a fourth constituent of gender, alongside the reformulated constituents of embodiment, representation and desire. Derived from this is a further concept of generative agency - the expression of the psychic construction of the self as potential procreator, shaped in childhood by the negotiation of reproductive restrictions of sex, generation, genesis and generativity, and the ‘genitive’ issues of arbitrariness, finitude and irreversibility of time. Disturbances in generative identity manifest as unconscious ‘shadows’ expressed as inhibitions to creative agency, compulsively driven preoccupations with the lived sexed body, and/or concrete enactments which may utilize biotechnological innovations to actualize unconscious fantasies in reality.

Prophecy Coles

18 Spencer Road, Wandsworth, London SW18 2SW. [email: prophecy.c@virgin.net]

Prophecy Coles  

Sisters, Sibling Relationships, Transgenerational Conflicts, Sibling Transference, Countertransference, Lost Identity, Siblings in Literature

The first half of this paper reconsiders the therapeutic work with a patient who had a troubled relationship with her older sister (Coles 1998). In particular I explore the conflictual sibling transference and the countertransference anxieties I faced. In the second half of the paper I speculate about transgenerational conflicts between sisters and suggest that the patient's conflict with her sister, and her sense of lost identity when her sister died, may be linked to her mother's relationship with an older sister. I draw on literary sources which also illustrate the impact of sibling relationships.

Paul Williams  

The author reflects upon the nature and process of generating original thought using examples from psychoanalysis, anthropology, poetry, art and ordinary life. The capacity to remain open to preconscious and unconscious influences, and to be able to mentally represent these, is deemed essential for the generation of thought, as opposed to reflexive thinking and mimesis. The conditions for this generative, dialectical mental activity are considered. Through a clinical example of a psychoanalytic treatment of a highly disturbed young man, processes of destruction of generative thought by psychosis are discussed, and what is required for this destructive activity to be halted and reversed. Paramount amongst the analyst's forms of engagement with the patient is the employment of intuition as a means of identifying unconscious truths and of creating the conditions for a ‘third’ analytic position without which the growth of mind is not possible.

Mother Courage: Reflections on Maternal Resilience

Lisa Baraitser PHD and Amélie Noack

Amélie Noack

London WC1E 7HX. [email: l.baraitser@bbk.ac.uk]

1 Daleham Gardens, London NW3 5BY. [email: AmelieNoac@aol.com]

Amélie Noack  

This paper attempts to develop a psychoanalytic perspective on maternal resilience. It argues that notions of resilience have been largely focused on the development of resilience in children, with the mother being viewed as a key figure in understanding its success or failure. However, the development of maternal resilience - the capacity for mothers to survive the vicissitudes of the parenting experience itself - has received less attention, occluding an important aspect of maternal subjectivity. Drawing on recent work on maternal ambivalence, this paper explores the relation between ambivalence and resilience, and provides clinical material from a two-year slow-open analytic group for mothers at the Maya Centre to illustrate our view that maternal resilience may usefully describe the aspect of ambivalence that entails bearing and accepting ourselves as mothers as well as our ambivalent feelings about our children.

New Psychoanalytic Theories of Female and Male Femininity: The Oedipus Complex, Language and Gender Embodiment

Marie Maguire and Hilary Dewing

Hilary Dewing

6 Stockwell Park Road, London SW9 0AJ. [email: mariemaguire2000@aol.com]

30 Pickets Street, London SW12 8QB. [email: hilary.dewing@btinternet.com]

Hilary Dewing  

Femininity; Oedipus Complex; Symbolic; Gender Embodiment; Sexual Identity

This edited interview explores the clinical applications of recent critiques of oedipal theories of ‘femininity’. We discuss new thinking about language, sexuality and how we symbolize gender through our bodies, illustrating the influence of neuro-psychoanalysis (Solms & Turnbull 2002) and post-Lacanian theory (Irigaray 1977; Grosz 1994). Radical challenges to the use of ‘binary’ categories, including masculinity/femininity, are considered, and we note that dispensing with such terminology impedes discussion of gender inequality. We explore intersubjective (Benjamin 2000) and philosophical (Butler 2000) perspectives on gender as the site for enactments of trauma (Harris 2000), along with the role of unmourned loss in the creation of heterosexual femininity. Clinical examples are counterposed: contemporary theory on male ‘femininity’ and hysteria, with recent thinking about female ‘masculinity’. We conclude that we may be reaching an impasse - the end of a golden age of theorizing about sexual identity - because of the current limitations and contradictions of psychoanalytic language and theory.

This paper examines ways in which Matte Blanco's ideas can be used to link psychodynamic and cognitive behavioural theories. This paper considers the notion of resilience in the context of the psychodynamics of bullying. It draws a distinction between the role and function of group membership on the one hand and of gang formations on the other. The ‘safety in numbers’ mentality establishes a false sense of integration and identity, especially attractive to those whose early experiences have undermined their resilience as a result of insufficient containment, of aggressive and hostile impulses above all. The paper argues that resilience is the capacity to withstand destructive impulses and experiences and that that capacity is lodged in very early development. It draws on Bion's theories in particular, and offers examples from infant and young child observations.

Mary Thomas

Mary Thomas

London

Mary Thomas  

The passage of time, and the ways that we and our patients deny, resist and defend against this, is a major theme in this fascinating collection of Pearl King's papers, written between 1951-2004. Alongside her psychoanalytic thinking she draws on reflections on time in poetry, especially in T.S. Eliot's work, from whose poem, ‘Burnt Norton’, she takes the title of this book. Psychoanalytic work occupies a paradoxical relationship with time, operating both in time and out of time. As Ken Robinson observes in his Introduction, ‘The psychoanalytic session is structured in time but represents a sort of playground out of time or, as Freud described it, “an intermediate region between illness and real life through which the transition from one to the other is made”’ (p. 11).

The book is divided into three sections. The first section explores some important clinical issues including the use of the analyst's affective response to the patient in developing our understanding of the transference and countertransference in clinical practice, the interplay between psychoanalytic theory, trauma and developmental thinking, and the analytic attitude as a curative factor. This section starts with Pearl King's account of her analysis of a 4-year-old boy who came into treatment after witnessing his younger brother falling to his death from a window. Brett Kahr, in his Foreword, observes that her work with this young boy established King as a pioneer in the study of trauma in the 1950s, and also that this is one of the longest follow-up studies of a psychoanalytic treatment in the literature. King gives a very engaging account of her analysis of ‘Philip’ who was referred to her by Winnicott in 1951. Winnicott also supervised her on this case which was her first child analysis. She conveys how she entered into Philip's world, allowing him to use her like a toy, and enabling him to act out some of his destructiveness, as he was too traumatized and anxious to be able to play. When the analysis ended she kept up some contact with Philip by sending him cards and a five-shilling postal order every Christmas. He returned to see her for three sessions when he was 14 and they kept in touch with each other for over 50 years by exchanging Christmas cards. When she wrote up her work with him she invited him to read it and respond. The chapter ends with Philip's postscript in which he acknowledges his gratitude for Pearl King's work with him, and how it enabled him to work through some of his early difficulties and to carve out a fulfilling life for himself.

Mary Target PHD

Mary Target

21 Maresfield Gardens, London NW3 5SD. [email: m.target@ucl.ac.uk]

Mary Target  

Sexuality, Psychosexuality, Object Relations, Laplanche, Drive Theory, Attachment Theory

Psychoanalytic theory, with its move away from drive theory to object-relations, lacks a compatible model of the power of psychosexuality in adult life (including in therapy). It is proposed that in infancy drive tension, frustration and urgency may be erotized by the caregiver; while actual sexual excitement may remain unmirrored and uncontained. This produces a psychosexual core which is unstable, elusive and never felt to be really owned. In sexual acts we can project and identify with our own sexuality, felt to belong to the other, yet allowing more successful re-internalization and gradual integration. The relief at being able to relate to troubling aspects of the self, via the other, creates a deep attachment bond, although sexual excitement may fade as self-integration becomes more secure. The technical challenges of working on sexuality in long-term, relationship-focused psychotherapy with an implicit parental model are briefly considered.

This paper describes enactments in the countertransference - spanning fantasies, actions, words and sexual responses to patients. It will explore the origins and reverberations of the analyst's enactments in an effort to understand whether they have obstructed progress or created special moments in the therapy where shifts in the patients' inner world, or further understanding on the part of the analyst could be created.

Clinical vignettes will be used from work with several patients, although the analyst will focus mainly on work with patients who present with hysterical personality. The paper is an endeavour to tease out what, if any, differences there may be in working with hysterical patients, as opposed to patients with other personality types, in the nature of countertransference enactments. The author examines the role of rescue fantasies in the c reation of an enactment.

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves

Gorseacre, West Polberro, St. Agnes, Cornwall TR5 OST. [email: reeves.gorseacre@btinternet.com]

Christopher Reeves  

This paper considers the initial negative reaction to Winnicott's paper ‘On the use of an object’ in the light of its author's own reservations about it. It argues that its obscurities indicate Winnicott's own difficulties in articulating how the young child moves from subjectivity to the objective apprehension of the external world, and the part played in it by aggression. Particular attention is paid to Winnicott's interest in certain late texts of Freud where the ‘death instinct’ (Todestrieb) features prominently. It is suggested that Winnicott's interest, like Freud's, was prompted by the ambition of moving beyond psychopathology to formulate the outlines of a developmental psychology. Again like Freud it is argued that in this endeavour he was conceptually overreaching himself, though for different reasons. The paper concludes with some considerations about the inherently dual nature of any would-be comprehensive psychology of human understanding and behaviour, and of the necessarily partial contribution of psychodynamic theorizing towards it. The search for such a unitary psychoanalytic formula is what unites the two men.

Marguerite Valentine  

While the film The Night Porter, which was originally released in 1974, ostensibly portrays a detailed account of the development of a sadomasochistic relationship, it may also be read as a political metaphor. The film's director and writer, Liliana Cavani, explicitly links the two protagonists' obsession with each other as originating in an earlier shared experience within a concentration camp. This is to become re-enacted years later following a chance meeting. This paper is a detailed psychoanalytic exposition of the development and nature of that relationship, but read within the context of a political and sociological framework. It notes how Cavani uses visual symbolization to represent the increasing perverse control and symbiotic complicity between Max, the Nazi guard, and Lucia, the young Jewish woman. The film's power lies in the implicit: it is an allegory of a society's descent into barbarism, and a portentous critique of authoritarianism, however expressed.

The title of this book raises the old question of whether psychoanalysis should be classified as science or art. Coming as I do from a scientific background and having recently reviewed a book for this Journal that assumes that psychoanalysis has advanced - and should advance - by subjecting its claims to scientific test, I find myself struggling to integrate the two perspectives. Ogden himself seems to succeed in this task, for instance, by combining a masterly examination of Freud's ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ paper (claiming to find there the genesis of the idea of an internal object, and therefore of object relations theory) with frequent citing of poems and poetical insights by Borges and Frost. This book is the fifth in a series that started in 2002 on psychoanalysis and women, and the fourth to have been edited by Alcira Mariam Alizade. Such an editorial pace may have taken its toll; there are some omissions and

604

repetitions in the texts and on occasion the papers seem to suffer from having been reduced from extended versions published elsewhere. That said, there is also much to commend it. The book comprises a collection of 16 essays by analysts from different parts of the world. The geographical, economic and social reach makes for diversity, not only in terms of thinking about motherhood, but also of ways of using theoretical constructs, and this is refreshing in itself. This is not a book to be read at one sitting. It takes time and attention to find the way into each contributor's idiom, but this book provides much food for thought and requires no specialist interest in perinatal psychology and psychopathology to appreciate its scope.

In her brief foreword, Alcira Mariam Alizade writes, ‘This book takes a fresh look at women in their maternal role - in order to highlight the hitherto unknown aspects to which social and cultural change have given rise’ (p. ix). For psychoanalysis the crucial question is the way in which social and cultural change, and scientific advance, are refracted through individual psychic structure and unconscious phantasy. But when she continues, ‘Not all twenty-first century mothers treat motherhood in accordance with the established model’ (p. ix), I was puzzled. One of the meanings of the ‘established’ model might be that up until quite recently it has taken the sexual act between a live and fertile man and woman to produce a baby. Now this is not necessarily the case. IVF, surrogacy, egg and sperm storage and donation, hormonal intervention and so on have extended what is possible for women, hetero- and homosexual couples, who seek motherhood. Joan Raphael-Leff writes, ‘Mothers (and fathers, too) are now freer to follow their own unconscious representations and desires, for better or worse’ (p. 147). Another possible deviation from the established model, which Estela Welldon addresses in her paper ‘Why Do You Want to have a Child?’ might be that ‘Motherhood … could at times be used unconsciously as a vehicle for perverse designs’ (p. 60).

Melanie Hart

Melanie Hart

1 Offerton Road, London SW4 0DH. [email: melaniehart@dial.pipex.com]

Melanie Hart  

This painting prompted me to wonder whether it is possible to find the capacities and structures of the mind, as described by psychoanalysis, represented unconsciously in visual form. I explain why this exceptional painting seems to be one worth exploring for this purpose and, although there are myriad ways of approaching such a rich work of art, lay particular stress on its abstract, structural aspects. Doing this seems to reveal that Titian would have had no difficulty in understanding psychoanalytic formulations about mental structure had anyone been able to describe them to him verbally. Perhaps the human mind records its own activity, and understands itself, at a depth we have not understood.

Steven Flower  

There have been many debates about psychoanalytic and Jungian views of homosexuality. As part of these it has often been recognized that analysts have appeared reluctant to comment on their own countertransference responses to gay patients. Yet these responses must inevitably have a significant bearing on the way the work is conceptualized and undertaken. This paper highlights ways in which homophobia and related countertransference difficulties influenced the author's ability to engage with one male patient. It traces the process by which the analyst became aware of his own discomfort and the nature of his struggle to find a more helpful and reflective position in the analytic work. The process was prompted by a dream which depicted some of the difficulties the analytic pair was experiencing and by a heightened scrutiny of the countertransference. The progress of the work is marked by three further dreams which trace the development of the analytic relationship.

One notable aspect of femininity is the two-fold higher rate of depression among women. This paper outlines bio-psychosocial models of depression and draws on studies of depressive disorder directly comparing men and women. Vreni Gould

Vreni Gould

London

Vreni Gould  

In the Spring 2001 issue (vol. 17, no. 3) the BJP published the seventh Annual John Bowlby Memorial Lecture given by Allan Schore in March 2000 with the title ‘Minds in the Making’. The dialogue between neuroscience, attachment theory and psychoanalysis has since gathered momentum with the publication of numerous books and papers. Margaret Wilkinson's book which includes a foreword by Allan Schore is a welcome and important addition. It makes cutting-edge research accessible and offers a lucid overview of contemporary neuroscience. Yet at the same time Wilkinson puts clinical material at the heart of her book. Each chapter contains clinical examples which help to bridge the gap between theory and practice, and in true Jungian style she includes nine coloured plates of pictures produced by her patients during analysis. It is this emphasis on the clinical relevance of neuroscience which makes this book of great interest to Jungian analysts, psychoanalytic psychotherapists and counsellors alike. Clinical material is presented in a different type-face which I found helpful.

In the first chapter ‘Why Neuroscience?’ Wilkinson argues that, thanks to recent developments in the field of neuroscience, we as practitioners are now better able to understand why we do what we do in the consulting room. A recurring theme is how neuroscience is contributing to our knowledge of how human subjectivity (coming into mind) is formed developmentally, initially through the relation to the primary care-giver. Mind is made by the healthy interaction with another mind. The patterns of the early attachment, laid down in the right hemisphere of the brain, are recreated in the relationship with the analyst as transference and countertransference. It is the understanding of these patterns which will be crucial for effective work to occur at a rational level (connecting right brain to left).

Perceptions of Gender Ideals Predict Outcome of Eating Disorders in Adolescent Girls

Barbro Thurfjell, Mona Eliasson, Ingemar Swenne, Anne-Liis von Knorring and Ingemar Engström

Clinical features have low predictive value for the outcome of eating disorders. This study focuses on the possible predictive value of gender ideals. Data was from adolescent girls thoroughly assessed both at presentation and at a three-year follow up. Few variables differed between the outcome groups. However, perceptions of gender ideals, as measured by the Three Questions of Ideals, were found to contribute to the prediction of outcome. A discriminant analysis showed that gender ideals, maturity fears, sexual debut and vomiting were significant discriminators in a set of factors, which correctly classified the outcome for 75.3% of the sample.



International Forum of Psychoanalysis15, 70-80, 2006

Deconstructing the Unconscious Saboteur: Composing a Life with Ambition and Desire

Harriet Kimble Wrye

This paper explores the unconscious roots of women's ambition from an object relations, developmental and hermeneutic perspective. Three high-profile women's stories illustrate the formative and deformative power of narration: those of Hilary Clinton, Tina Turner and the heroine of Phantom of the Opera. Each narrative reveals typical deformative constrictions to the expression of female ambition, including male abrogation of female capability and the denigration of ambition as unfeminine. Through clinical vignettes, this paper explores dynamic, developmental and cultural forces that block female ambition's full flowering. Part of the need to keep women's ambition limited stems from the unconscious needs of the masculine psyche for superiority. This is communicated to little girls through their mothers' internalized parental imagos, including their mothers' identification with their mothers and their own oedipal struggles. Similarly, the father's unconscious anxieties in relation to his parental imagos, particularly his preoedipal and oedipal relations with his mother, are communicated. Another constraining dynamic relates to female conflicts around separation from the mother. Composing new narratives of women's ambition with our patients can incorporate the uniquely feminine aspects of comfort with diffusion, while weaving multiple and disparate strands laced with nurturance and aggression.
